nodes.label: 1% on price beats 1% on acquisition — you raise prices too little and too late
nodes.norm_label: 1% on price beats 1% on acquisition — you raise prices too little and too late
nodes.rationale: A 1% price improvement drives ~8–11% more profit (ProfitWell) on typical SaaS margins, while a 1% acquisition improvement yields ~2%. Yet 70% of executives rank acquisition as the most important growth lever — the one that pays least. Price is left untouched because of loss aversion (fear of losing what you have screams louder than the chance to gain).
nodes.source_location: section: 1% on price beats 1% on acquisition — you raise prices too little and too late

nodes.label: Ask for the card in trial — but optimize for the right ICP, not raw conversion
nodes.norm_label: ask for the card in trial — but optimize for the right icp, not raw conversion
nodes.rationale: Requiring a credit card multiplies trial-to-paid conversion but shrinks signups; the goal is the model that attracts and retains the right ICP, not the one with the highest headline conversion.
nodes.source_location: section: Ask for the card in trial — but optimize for the right ICP, not raw conversion

nodes.label: Build a single value axis, then tune the decoy's distance to your target plan
nodes.norm_label: build a single value axis, then tune the decoy's distance to your target plan
nodes.rationale: A plan ladder must read as one clear progression of value; mixing quantitative and qualitative axes muddles it, and where you place the decoy's price decides which plan looks like the deal.
nodes.source_location: section: Build a single value axis, then tune the decoy's distance to your target plan

nodes.label: Competing on price is adverse selection — you filter in the worst client
nodes.norm_label: competing on price is adverse selection — you filter in the worst client
nodes.rationale: Price-led copycats attract bargain hunters: they enter because you're cheapest and leave the second someone is R$1 cheaper. High churn, zero loyalty, most support tickets. Price as bait is a filter for the client you least want. Better: Kawasaki's "Be a baker, not an eater" — bake your own pie via niche (CRM for facial-aesthetics clinics, not another CRM) and charge 5x with no comparison. Use the giant's weight against it (jiu-jitsu): big players' blind spots are in public complaints — ReclameAqui, app stores, Google Places, communities, FB/WhatsApp groups, niche sites. Each complainer represents ~26 equally unhappy silent ones.
nodes.source_location: section: Competing on price is adverse selection — you filter in the worst client

nodes.label: Engineer the comparison frame with a decoy and a high anchor — and drop Free from the top
nodes.norm_label: engineer the comparison frame with a decoy and a high anchor — and drop free from the top
nodes.rationale: Conversion shifts when you change the frame of comparison, not the product; equal-looking options cause delay, and showing Free first anchors everyone to zero so everything else feels expensive.
nodes.source_location: section: Engineer the comparison frame with a decoy and a high anchor — and drop Free from the top

nodes.label: Engineer the pricing page with Good-Better-Best and control the comparison
nodes.norm_label: engineer the pricing page with good-better-best and control the comparison
nodes.rationale: Lost LTV is rarely about price — it's analysis paralysis from a missing choice architecture. The brain is lazy and judges by relative comparison (priming + anchoring), so if you don't design the anchor, users compare you to "nothing" or to the cheapest competitor.
nodes.source_location: section: Engineer the pricing page with Good-Better-Best and control the comparison

nodes.label: Frame the upgrade as a loss at the moment of value, not a feature you're selling
nodes.norm_label: frame the upgrade as a loss at the moment of value, not a feature you're selling
nodes.rationale: Low upgrade rates are usually a framing-and-timing problem, not a price problem; remind users what they've already invested and what they stand to lose.
nodes.source_location: section: Frame the upgrade as a loss at the moment of value, not a feature you're selling

nodes.label: Make the middle plan the one you actually want to sell
nodes.norm_label: make the middle plan the one you actually want to sell
nodes.rationale: Each plan has a behavioral job, not just a price; the plan you most want to sell should sit in the middle, flanked by a decoy below and an anchor above.
nodes.source_location: section: Make the middle plan the one you actually want to sell

nodes.label: Order pricing rows by the serial-position effect: killer feature first, differentiator last
nodes.norm_label: order pricing rows by the serial-position effect: killer feature first, differentiator last
nodes.rationale: Users don't read pricing lists linearly; attention and memory cluster on the first and last items, so feature order is itself a conversion lever.
nodes.source_location: section: Order pricing rows by the serial-position effect: killer feature first, differentiator last

nodes.label: Price from cost+margin floor and value ceiling — never tarot or competitor-minus-20%
nodes.norm_label: price from cost+margin floor and value ceiling — never tarot or competitor-minus-20%
nodes.rationale: Two calculations give your floor and ceiling. Floor = cost to serve + target margin (infra, support, tools, tokens; if R$10/account and 80% margin, floor is R$50). But two traps: price too low signals low quality before use, and CAC math can eat the margin (CAC R$100 + margin R$40/mo = 2.5-month payback; churn at month 3 = you worked 3 months for R$20). Ceiling = reference value — what the client pays today to solve it their way (Excel + 1.5h/day of admin; or the loss they absorb by not solving).
nodes.source_location: section: Price from cost+margin floor and value ceiling — never tarot or competitor-minus-20%

nodes.label: Price is the cheapest money — stop anchoring it to the cheapest competitor
nodes.norm_label: price is the cheapest money — stop anchoring it to the cheapest competitor
nodes.rationale: Pricing is a SaaS's biggest lever, yet ~90% of products are underpriced — the founder, who knows every limitation, anchors on the cheapest competitor instead of on value delivered. The buyer only sees the problem solved.
nodes.source_location: section: Price is the cheapest money — stop anchoring it to the cheapest competitor

nodes.label: The freemium trap, in numbers: higher conversion, far lower cash
nodes.norm_label: the freemium trap, in numbers: higher conversion, far lower cash
nodes.rationale: A free plan lifts signup conversion but can crush the economics — the higher top-of-funnel number hides a worse business.
nodes.source_location: section: The freemium trap, in numbers: higher conversion, far lower cash

nodes.label: Tie the trial's end to value consumed, not the calendar
nodes.norm_label: tie the trial's end to value consumed, not the calendar
nodes.rationale: Blocking access on a fixed day count (7/14/28) is a lazy rule; the billing trigger should fire on value consumption, after the user's first real win.
nodes.source_location: section: Tie the trial's end to value consumed, not the calendar

nodes.label: Use a disfluent font for genuine deals — and name tiers for the mix you want
nodes.norm_label: use a disfluent font for genuine deals — and name tiers for the mix you want
nodes.rationale: A uniformly polished pricing page can be easy to scan yet weak at selling. For a genuinely favorable promotion, a disfluent (ugly) font on the price can make people process the number more deeply. Tier labels can change purchase incidence and which tier buyers choose — and those effects can run in opposite directions.
nodes.source_location: section: Use a disfluent font for genuine deals — and name tiers for the mix you want

nodes.label: Whether freemium works is decided by the cost to serve a free user
nodes.norm_label: whether freemium works is decided by the cost to serve a free user
nodes.rationale: Freemium isn't good or bad in the abstract — the *cost of free* decides, and it hinges on (1) how much it costs to serve non-payers and (2) how long/expensive activation is.
nodes.source_location: section: Whether freemium works is decided by the cost to serve a free user

nodes.rationale: A product hired to solve a one-off problem generates structural churn: a user who loves it and still cancels isn't unhappy — they finished the job they came to do, and there was no continuous value to bring them back.

nodes.label: Churn and payback are one problem, measured in two places
nodes.norm_label: churn and payback are one problem, measured in two places

nodes.label: Churn math: restructured onboarding can preserve R$4.8k MRR from an existing base
nodes.norm_label: churn math: restructured onboarding can preserve r$4.8k mrr from an existing base
nodes.rationale: 6% churn on 900 users at R$300 ARPU is 54 cancellations, or R$16.2k MRR, leaving each month. Restructured onboarding (contextual welcome + empty state + activation checklist) cut cancellations by ~30%: about 16 accounts retained, preserving R$4.8k MRR — a R$57.6k ARR run-rate or R$52.8k over the post's stated 11-month average lifetime. No new traffic, no new feature.
nodes.source_location: section: Churn math: restructured onboarding can preserve R$4.8k MRR from an existing base

nodes.label: Churn starts on the landing page, not at cancel
nodes.norm_label: churn starts on the landing page, not at cancel
nodes.rationale: If the LP promises one thing and the product delivers another, you create an expectation debt that charges interest every day the user thinks "this isn't what I expected" — and the disappointment is pre-programmed even if the product is excellent.
nodes.source_location: section: Churn starts on the landing page, not at cancel

nodes.label: Design the cancel screen — it's your last conversation, not a form
nodes.norm_label: design the cancel screen — it's your last conversation, not a form
nodes.rationale: The cancellation screen is the most ignored yet one of the most important pages in the product; treating it as a bureaucratic form wastes your final chance to retain.
nodes.source_location: section: Design the cancel screen — it's your last conversation, not a form

nodes.label: Engineer addiction like a game so CS isn't a churn tax
nodes.norm_label: engineer addiction like a game so cs isn't a churn tax
nodes.rationale: Customer Success is the tax you pay for a non-addictive product — if you need an army of CSMs to stop cancellations, the product failed. Your real competitor isn't another startup; it's boredom, and boredom has infinite CAC. The CNPJ buying your SaaS is the same brain that plays Candy Crush; reward neuroscience is identical. Win retention across three game-design phases.
nodes.source_location: section: Engineer addiction like a game so CS isn't a churn tax

nodes.label: Retention is raising the cost of leaving day after day — iFood's behavioral lock-in
nodes.norm_label: retention is raising the cost of leaving day after day — ifood's behavioral lock-in
nodes.rationale: iFood isn't just a business model — it's Brazil's most sophisticated behavioral lock-in. Each layer (delivery, data, credit, card) raises the psychological and operational cost of leaving: sunk-cost effect plus ecosystem dependency. The restaurant doesn't stay because iFood is good; it stays because leaving got too expensive. Retention isn't a feature — it's the accumulated cost of exit.
nodes.source_location: section: Retention is raising the cost of leaving day after day — iFood's behavioral lock-in

nodes.label: Strip the jargon before you blame onboarding
nodes.norm_label: strip the jargon before you blame onboarding
nodes.rationale: Churn that looks like a product problem is often a language problem: a technical founder writes product and sales copy in jargon, the ICP buys on a leap of faith, never perceives value, accumulates small disappointments, and cancels — looking like a missing feature on the dashboard.
nodes.source_location: section: Strip the jargon before you blame onboarding

nodes.label: Switching cost is what turns months of LTV into years
nodes.norm_label: switching cost is what turns months of ltv into years
nodes.rationale: The same product, designed differently, yields months vs. years of LTV. Switching cost = the effort a user *perceives* in leaving; low switching cost means thin history and an easy exit.
nodes.source_location: section: Switching cost is what turns months of LTV into years

nodes.label: Tell the existing base about upgrades before they want to leave
nodes.norm_label: tell the existing base about upgrades before they want to leave
nodes.rationale: Reactive improvement communication is a sneaky churn vector: if you only market new versions to cold traffic to avoid cannibalizing the old product, your base assumes the old version is the ceiling and leaves when a competitor looks better.
nodes.source_location: section: Tell the existing base about upgrades before they want to leave

nodes.label: The 3 biggest churn reasons — and the fix for each
nodes.norm_label: the 3 biggest churn reasons — and the fix for each
nodes.rationale: Most churn traces to three causes, each with a distinct fix. (1) Bad onboarding → gradual guided immersion to what users value most, a Zeigarnik progress bar (incompleteness nags), and targeted tooltips on unexplored features. (2) Missing perceived value → show user ROI in a simple dashboard (Grammarly shows words helped), promote feature discovery continuously, build community. (3) Hard/confusing interface → fix via a proper product design project.
nodes.source_location: section: The 3 biggest churn reasons — and the fix for each

nodes.label: The funnel leaks at three points — diagnose which before fixing
nodes.norm_label: the funnel leaks at three points — diagnose which before fixing
nodes.rationale: The three most common SaaS funnel holes for Brazilian founders: (1) cancel in month 1–2 → onboarding missing or LP promised the wrong thing (brought off-ICP users); the first is a product problem (shorten path to value), the second marketing (tighten the promise). (2) Many trials, few paid → paywall at the wrong moment or a broken value ladder. (3) Many visits, few signups → confused ICP and/or generic value proposition — but check the acquisition source first; wrong traffic can't be saved by copy.
nodes.source_location: section: The funnel leaks at three points — diagnose which before fixing

nodes.label: Treat support volume as a design problem, not a staffing one
nodes.norm_label: treat support volume as a design problem, not a staffing one
nodes.rationale: What looks like a support problem is usually a design problem — you cut ticket volume during onboarding itself, with an interface that answers questions before they're asked. Low-ticket digital products generate up to 3x more support than conventional tickets.
nodes.source_location: section: Treat support volume as a design problem, not a staffing one

nodes.label: 94% of features are filler — Pendo's data and what to do about it
nodes.norm_label: 94% of features are filler — pendo's data and what to do about it
nodes.rationale: Pendo's analysis across ~2,500 companies' apps found roughly 6% feature adoption in the average product; even top-10% products reached only 15.6%. That leaves about 94% rarely or never used in the average product (84.4% even in the top decile), creating low activation, churn, a larger attack surface, and higher sustaining cost/complexity. Some features sell without being used, but that doesn't explain the gap.
nodes.source_location: section: 94% of features are filler — Pendo's data and what to do about it

nodes.label: Building is the comfort zone; distribution is the game
nodes.norm_label: building is the comfort zone; distribution is the game
nodes.rationale: Founders choose to build because selling hurts — Richard spent 90% of his time perfecting a delivery product one year before iFood existed; it died beautiful. Humane raised ~US$240M, ex-Apple founders, gorgeous hardware; returns outpaced sales by summer 2024 and HP took the assets for US$116M. In survival phase you do both jobs and almost always pick building — your comfort zone — pretending the next feature will make selling easier. Exercise: how many months of runway does your next feature cost?
nodes.source_location: section: Building is the comfort zone; distribution is the game

nodes.label: Compute your Swiss Knife Index to expose feature creep
nodes.norm_label: compute your swiss knife index to expose feature creep
nodes.rationale: A product's worth is measured by features actually used, not features shipped; a bloated product is expensive to sustain and hard to sell, not rich.
nodes.source_location: section: Compute your Swiss Knife Index to expose feature creep

nodes.label: Design the attention hierarchy to direct behavior, not just organize info
nodes.norm_label: design the attention hierarchy to direct behavior, not just organize info
nodes.rationale: A product that organizes delivers access; a product that directs delivers activation — and the visual hierarchy decides which the user gets.
nodes.source_location: section: Design the attention hierarchy to direct behavior, not just organize info

nodes.label: Feature adoption is a design problem, not a communication problem
nodes.norm_label: feature adoption is a design problem, not a communication problem
nodes.rationale: Shipping a feature doesn't make it discovered; users move through their habitual path and never see what they aren't looking for.
nodes.source_location: section: Feature adoption is a design problem, not a communication problem

nodes.label: Feature creep ("fiturite") is a business cost, not just a UX one
nodes.norm_label: feature creep ("fiturite") is a business cost, not just a ux one
nodes.rationale: The Homer Simpson car problem: every unsatisfied user request implemented as a feature eventually makes the product hard to operate, steepens the learning curve, and worsens experience through cognitive overload and choice paradox. It's bad for the business too — you spend more on dev for features serving few users, more on maintenance, eventually whole teams for barely-needed areas. Prune based on: who are our most strategic users, what are they using, what's unused that I can abstract, what aligns with the vision.
nodes.source_location: section: Feature creep ("fiturite") is a business cost, not just a UX one

nodes.label: Feature requests from cancellations don't buy features
nodes.norm_label: feature requests from cancellations don't buy features
nodes.rationale: Three auto shops canceled RepareCar over missing boleto (bank-slip) issuance — request logged in Linear with name and date, 20+ in the same queue, oldest since June. But cancellation doesn't buy a feature: the ICP profile is defined, and boleto sits in a deliberately-not-doing package. Support is semi-automated (AI triages, human on novel questions, both open Linear tickets; a daily Claude task prioritizes). Bugs jump the queue; anything new defaults to parking lot.
nodes.source_location: section: Feature requests from cancellations don't buy features

nodes.label: Focus on your core; trying to be "all-in-one" dilutes your value proposition
nodes.norm_label: focus on your core; trying to be "all-in-one" dilutes your value proposition
nodes.rationale: Chasing a bigger TAM by going generic destroys retention of your heavy users without converting new ones — the same roadmap mistake in cars and in software.
nodes.source_location: section: Focus on your core; trying to be "all-in-one" dilutes your value proposition

nodes.label: Ground feature discipline in the academic feature-fatigue research
nodes.norm_label: ground feature discipline in the academic feature-fatigue research
nodes.rationale: Past a cognitive-load threshold, the subjective evaluation of a product doesn't stay neutral — it declines into frustration, confusion, and task abandonment, directly hitting CAC and LTV.
nodes.source_location: section: Ground feature discipline in the academic feature-fatigue research

nodes.label: Maturing the product means doing the same thing better, not adding power-user features
nodes.norm_label: maturing the product means doing the same thing better, not adding power-user features
nodes.rationale: Technical founders keep densifying the product for heavy users, making it expensive, complex, and hard for the average user — a Boeing 747 cockpit. Maturing means doing better what the product already does: smoother flows, bug fixes, attention direction. Hidden risk: a power-user product has a smaller top of funnel, so you must charge more — you changed markets (TAM/SAM changed) and price must follow. The founder then reads "product is bad" when really ICP isn't adjusted. Adjust copy (more executive, less tool-like), visuals (show the result, less product internals), and detail care (high-paying ICP tolerates AI-slop design less).
nodes.source_location: section: Maturing the product means doing the same thing better, not adding power-user features

nodes.label: Past the optimal feature count, a technically bigger product becomes functionally worse
nodes.norm_label: past the optimal feature count, a technically bigger product becomes functionally worse
nodes.rationale: The relationship between feature count and perceived utility is non-linear: there's an optimal point, after which each added feature reduces perceived utility while raising sustaining cost and the learning curve.
nodes.source_location: section: Past the optimal feature count, a technically bigger product becomes functionally worse

nodes.label: PMF is step 8 in a 10-step sequence — founders start there too early
nodes.norm_label: pmf is step 8 in a 10-step sequence — founders start there too early
nodes.rationale: Sequence: (1) Define the ICP — does it really exist, or is it who you wish it were? (2) Surface the ICP's pains and desires — real? verified where, with how many? (3) Understand awareness level — knows the pain? the solution? yours? (4) Slice niche/sub-niche — their particularities, do they exclude each other? (5) Size TAM of niche and sub — enough market, and does enough remain after niching? (6) Actively decide who the solution serves — can you stand out there? (7) Validate the thesis — the ICP's pain solved in a way that pays; are they paying? (8) Reach PMF — does the product stick? do users recommend it unprompted? does the business sustain itself without you pushing? (9) Fix inefficiencies in acquisition, activation, retention — always leaks; measured where? (10) Scale.
nodes.source_location: section: PMF is step 8 in a 10-step sequence — founders start there too early

nodes.label: Run every feature through a two-layer "Swiss Knife filter" before building
nodes.norm_label: run every feature through a two-layer "swiss knife filter" before building
nodes.rationale: A feature you ship stays forever and charges rent forever, so the right question isn't "is this good?" but "does it deserve the permanent cost it imposes on the product?"
nodes.source_location: section: Run every feature through a two-layer "Swiss Knife filter" before building

nodes.label: (Earlier draft) The 10 design principles
nodes.rationale: An earlier morning draft of what later became the canonical RCD framework above — explicitly "focused on influencing behavior and generating revenue."

nodes.label: Better design wins even when the tech is worse
nodes.norm_label: better design wins even when the tech is worse
nodes.rationale: A competitor with worse technology still beats you when their onboarding is smoother, their copy clearer, their features easier, their error messages feel human, and their product feels like someone cared. That sum is "better design" — and it's why they're winning and you're not.
nodes.source_location: section: Better design wins even when the tech is worse

nodes.label: Design owns the flow, not the final coat of paint
nodes.norm_label: design owns the flow, not the final coat of paint
nodes.rationale: What decides whether a user converts or churns — information order, when you ask for the card, what appears at moments of doubt, when value is first felt — is set and coded long before a "finished" product reaches design.
nodes.source_location: section: Design owns the flow, not the final coat of paint

nodes.label: Design's leverage isn't constant — it changes with the product stage
nodes.norm_label: design's leverage isn't constant — it changes with the product stage
nodes.rationale: Design's payoff is near-zero at MVP and grows to decisive at scale; when a product is dying, design is the *last* place to look for the culprit. Knowing your stage tells you whether design moves the cash or is just vanity.
nodes.source_location: section: Design's leverage isn't constant — it changes with the product stage

nodes.label: Don't hire a designer to make software "pretty"
nodes.norm_label: don't hire a designer to make software "pretty"
nodes.rationale: Aesthetics is subjective, doesn't scale, and won't save a product from high churn. The interface's job is to steer user behavior toward a KPI; aesthetics is sometimes a by-product of that. Hiring design for looks is technical founders' biggest financial mistake.
nodes.source_location: section: Don't hire a designer to make software "pretty"

nodes.label: Find the leaks before you rebuild the bucket
nodes.norm_label: find the leaks before you rebuild the bucket
nodes.rationale: Products rarely die from one dramatic error; they bleed out as micro-disappointments accumulate across the journey until the user quits without quite knowing why. Patch the leaks instead of redesigning from scratch — a fraction of the effort for most of the gain.
nodes.source_location: section: Find the leaks before you rebuild the bucket

nodes.label: Leave the over-used parts alone; improve around them
nodes.norm_label: leave the over-used parts alone; improve around them
nodes.rationale: Heavily-used parts of a working product form a "cognitive map" — users memorized where everything is and which gesture does what — that is part of the product even if you never designed it intentionally. Redesigning it aggressively makes them pay a re-learning cost and signals you think you know better than they do.
nodes.source_location: section: Leave the over-used parts alone; improve around them

nodes.label: Make the dashboard answer "what do I do now?"
nodes.norm_label: make the dashboard answer "what do i do now?"
nodes.rationale: A dashboard is your software's front door, not NASA mission control. Cram it with colorful charts, five-decimal counters, and endless tables and the user takes a cognitive-overload beating, feels dumb, and churns. A good dashboard answers one question — "What do I do now to get more value?" — and that drives LTV.
nodes.source_location: section: Make the dashboard answer "what do I do now?"

nodes.label: Measure changes; don't argue from opinion
nodes.norm_label: measure changes; don't argue from opinion
nodes.rationale: "Change the color, swap the CTA, kill the pop-up" — and nobody tests anything. Faith in gut beats faith in data science. Product design is experimentation and analysis, not guesswork: if you don't test, how will you improve, and if you don't improve, you don't grow.
nodes.source_location: section: Measure changes; don't argue from opinion

nodes.label: Mine the tactical layer — it's the most under-explored
nodes.norm_label: mine the tactical layer — it's the most under-explored
nodes.rationale: Product design has three leverage drivers — Tactical → Organizational → Strategic. Strategic has the most asymmetric upside, but because everyone outsourced aesthetics to the same AI-generated UI kit, the tactical layer (aesthetics + function) became the most under-explored opportunity in the stack: lowest leverage in theory, highest return in practice, simply because nobody looks.
nodes.source_location: section: Mine the tactical layer — it's the most under-explored

nodes.label: Refactor to solve a real problem, not to repaint the wall
nodes.norm_label: refactor to solve a real problem, not to repaint the wall
nodes.rationale: Designers loop forever ("it's great → could be better → better → repeat"), refactoring UI like code. True refactoring waits for user feedback and changes what fixes a problem; repainting because the old color got boring is vanity that burns a week on pixel-perfect nobody asked for.
nodes.source_location: section: Refactor to solve a real problem, not to repaint the wall

nodes.label: The 9 principles of Revenue Centric Design (RCD)
nodes.norm_label: the 9 principles of revenue centric design (rcd)
nodes.rationale: Intentional design serves the user AND the business at once — value and revenue, not one or the other. Richard's canonical framework, named Revenue Centric Design (RCD), built after Dieter Rams' 10 laws (form/function) and Amber Case's Calm Technology (attention/context) — "neither taught me to think about revenue."
nodes.source_location: section: The 9 principles of Revenue Centric Design (RCD)

nodes.label: Treat the interface as data, not opinion
nodes.norm_label: treat the interface as data, not opinion
nodes.rationale: One kind of founder, when churn rises, opens analytics — maps where users stalled, hesitated, which screen preceded cancellation — and treats interface as data. The other debates color palettes in product meetings. One is building a company, the other a portfolio.
nodes.source_location: section: Treat the interface as data, not opinion

nodes.label: "Paint the button" is judging the last line of a long cascade
nodes.norm_label: "paint the button" is judging the last line of a long cascade
nodes.rationale: The visual layer of a landing page is the tip of a cascade that begins at the ICP — so "make it more colorful" critiques the *end* of a process as if it were the start.
nodes.source_location: section: "Paint the button" is judging the last line of a long cascade

nodes.label: Aim for 4.2–4.5 stars, not a perfect 5
nodes.norm_label: aim for 4.2–4.5 stars, not a perfect 5
nodes.rationale: A flawless rating reads as fake; consumers distrust unanimity. A profile that includes constructive criticism feels more authentic and converts better than pure praise.
nodes.source_location: section: Aim for 4.2–4.5 stars, not a perfect 5

nodes.label: Click triggers: one line of risk-reducing microcopy next to the CTA
nodes.norm_label: click triggers: one line of risk-reducing microcopy next to the cta
nodes.rationale: A single line of text reducing perceived risk can save conversion — in CRO these are "click triggers" (marketing calls it objection-breaking): "Lifetime guarantee," "Free shipping," "7 days free, no card." It's certainty placed on top of a known ICP doubt.
nodes.source_location: section: Click triggers: one line of risk-reducing microcopy next to the CTA

nodes.label: Compliments aren't validation — "what's missing for you to PIX now?" is
nodes.norm_label: compliments aren't validation — "what's missing for you to pix now?" is
nodes.rationale: Everyone loves your idea, nobody bought. Compliments are free and worth nothing (like your freemium). The simplest validation test: try to sell. If you can't close inside your ICP, ask directly: "Falta o que pra você fazer o PIX agora?" ("What's missing for you to send the PIX instant payment right now?") The pause reveals the truth — either the real objection (your build list) or excuses (the "loved it" was just politeness). Follow up: "If it had that, would you pay now?" Then do 20 sales this way.
nodes.source_location: section: Compliments aren't validation — "what's missing for you to PIX now?" is

nodes.label: Compress the decision window — shorten the path to action below the path to doubt
nodes.norm_label: compress the decision window — shorten the path to action below the path to doubt
nodes.rationale: The purchase decision is mostly made before checkout. Conversion is architecture: the user converts when the path to the action is shorter than the path to doubt, because every extra second of deliberation raises the odds they close the tab.
nodes.source_location: section: Compress the decision window — shorten the path to action below the path to doubt

nodes.label: Converting pages are often ugly — design for performance, not applause
nodes.norm_label: converting pages are often ugly — design for performance, not applause
nodes.rationale: There's an invisible war between branding (looking good in the screenshot) and performance (conversion, retention, expansion). The page that puts money in the till is often visually aggressive, text-heavy, and far from the Apple aesthetic founders dream of.
nodes.source_location: section: Converting pages are often ugly — design for performance, not applause

nodes.label: Cut CAC by filtering on the landing page, not the media
nodes.norm_label: cut cac by filtering on the landing page, not the media
nodes.rationale: High CAC is rarely a media problem — it's usually a filtering problem. The landing page can qualify leads before the form, killing deals that were never going to close.
nodes.source_location: section: Cut CAC by filtering on the landing page, not the media

nodes.label: Debug ICP and awareness level before touching design
nodes.norm_label: debug icp and awareness level before touching design
nodes.rationale: Conversion is context engineering — who arrives, with what pain, at what stage, needing what proof. Two invisible variables must be debugged before writing a line of code: the Who (ICP) and the When (awareness level). Visual design comes last.
nodes.source_location: section: Debug ICP and awareness level before touching design

nodes.label: Design the features page for skimming, not reading
nodes.norm_label: design the features page for skimming, not reading
nodes.rationale: Almost nobody reads your features page — they skim three bullets and hunt for a demo video. Design for that behavior (with the caveat that the more conscious, technical slice of your ICP *will* read the detail).
nodes.source_location: section: Design the features page for skimming, not reading

nodes.label: Don't clone the page — the converting layer is invisible
nodes.norm_label: don't clone the page — the converting layer is invisible
nodes.rationale: A converting sales page is the visible shell of an invisible system. Copying the layout copies what's cheapest to produce; the expensive part (research) stays invisible and gets left behind.
nodes.source_location: section: Don't clone the page — the converting layer is invisible

nodes.label: Fix contrast, layout, and trust before rewriting copy
nodes.norm_label: fix contrast, layout, and trust before rewriting copy
nodes.rationale: The brain processes three pre-verbal variables — contrast, on-screen placement, and trust — before it reads the words, and they usually move the needle more than any headline.
nodes.source_location: section: Fix contrast, layout, and trust before rewriting copy

nodes.label: Founder LP guide: platform doesn't matter, load time does; proof must outweigh the promise
nodes.norm_label: founder lp guide: platform doesn't matter, load time does; proof must outweigh the promise
nodes.rationale: Profits are more sensitive to conversions than to costs, and the landing page is often the first gate between a founder's product and its users. The platform matters less than speed, clarity, contrast, proof, and direct action.
nodes.source_location: section: Founder LP guide: platform doesn't matter, load time does; proof must outweigh the promise

nodes.label: Judge a landing page by conversion, not by beauty
nodes.norm_label: judge a landing page by conversion, not by beauty
nodes.rationale: A landing page isn't a beauty contest — it has one measurable job: qualify the user and lower CAC by turning traffic into revenue. Evaluating a static image with no context is nearly useless.
nodes.source_location: section: Judge a landing page by conversion, not by beauty

nodes.label: Match CTA microcopy to the funnel stage
nodes.norm_label: match cta microcopy to the funnel stage
nodes.rationale: Button text should change with the user's progress in the funnel — the verb matches the mental state at each stage. First interaction: "Descubra como funciona" ("See how it works"). Product page: "Quero esse produto" ("I want this product"). Checkout: "Finalizar minha compra" ("Complete my purchase"). Short (≤4 words), clear, directional. This discreet personalization raises perceived control, confidence, and conversion.
nodes.source_location: section: Match CTA microcopy to the funnel stage

nodes.label: No clicks out, plus brutal CTA contrast
nodes.norm_label: no clicks out, plus brutal cta contrast
nodes.rationale: For conversion you want little distraction and lots of redundancy. Any clickable element that leads off-page is lost conversion — no matter how prestigious the source.
nodes.source_location: section: No clicks out, plus brutal CTA contrast

nodes.label: Pass the 5-second test — lead with the problem, not the feature
nodes.norm_label: pass the 5-second test — lead with the problem, not the feature
nodes.rationale: A visitor scans your LP for ~5 seconds. If they can't answer what it does, who it's for, and why they should care, they leave — they won't stay to figure it out. Conversion begins on the first line.
nodes.source_location: section: Pass the 5-second test — lead with the problem, not the feature

nodes.label: Performance is conversion: 31% better LCP → +8% sales (Vodafone A/B)
nodes.norm_label: performance is conversion: 31% better lcp → +8% sales (vodafone a/b)
nodes.rationale: You can raise conversion before opening Figma — web performance is a conversion lever, not an engineering nicety. Vodafone Italy A/B tested web-vitals optimization (LCP 31% better than control, same offer/creative/screen, 100k clicks and 34k visits/day per variant, paid traffic): +8% sales, +15% lead-to-visit, +11% cart-to-visit.
nodes.source_location: section: Performance is conversion: 31% better LCP → +8% sales (Vodafone A/B)

nodes.label: Real humans outconvert models — banner blindness explains why
nodes.norm_label: real humans outconvert models — banner blindness explains why
nodes.rationale: Highrise, the 37signals CRM, tested homepage variants with different human figures; real users and actual team developers converted best on average — above stock-photo models. (37signals later became Basecamp.) Likely explanation: banner blindness — we learn to ignore what looks like advertising and give attention to what's organic or unusual.
nodes.source_location: section: Real humans outconvert models — banner blindness explains why

nodes.label: Scaling cold traffic is an honesty test for your page
nodes.norm_label: scaling cold traffic is an honesty test for your page
nodes.rationale: Conversion measured on warm audiences (existing followers) is inflated — they forgive the page's flaws. Only cold traffic reveals how much of your rate is the page versus borrowed trust.
nodes.source_location: section: Scaling cold traffic is an honesty test for your page

nodes.label: Specificity is the difference between decoration and persuasion
nodes.norm_label: specificity is the difference between decoration and persuasion
nodes.rationale: Generic LP copy gets discarded by the brain; specific messages are processed faster and generate more trust. A converting LP shows the *transformation* the product causes, not just what it does.
nodes.source_location: section: Specificity is the difference between decoration and persuasion

nodes.label: Test hero comprehension with a stranger from your ICP
nodes.norm_label: test hero comprehension with a stranger from your icp
nodes.rationale: The cheapest usability test nobody runs: show your LP hero to one person for 5 seconds, take it away, ask "What does this product do? For whom?" If they can't answer, the hero failed — no matter how pretty it is. In those seconds the brain asks three questions, almost in order: what is this → is this for me → why should I care now. The mechanism is cognitive load: every second spent decoding what you do is a second closer to giving up — clarity beats cleverness at the top of the funnel, always.
nodes.source_location: section: Test hero comprehension with a stranger from your ICP

nodes.label: The 2026 landing page checklist
nodes.rationale: An all-in-one checklist for a converting LP — @namyakhann's (Supafast) list, which Richard translated and endorsed in full: Hero (1 clear promise / 1 specific audience / 1 exact-action CTA / show-don't-explain visual / trust seal above the fold). Copy (headline <10 words, benefit before feature, customer language, one central transformation, scannable in 5s). Social proof (logos if you have names, metrics if you have traction, specific result testimonials, zero generic praise). Structure (Hero → Pain → Solution → Proof → CTA; max 3 feature sections; FAQ kills top 5 objections; CTA repeated 2–3x). Technical (<3s load, real mobile-first, single-scroll flow).

nodes.label: Users scan, they don't read — give the primary action obvious contrast
nodes.norm_label: users scan, they don't read — give the primary action obvious contrast
nodes.rationale: Users scan interfaces, weighing cognitive effort against payoff, and ignore most of it. They enter with one question — "What can I do here?" — so the primary action must win on contrast within seconds.
nodes.source_location: section: Users scan, they don't read — give the primary action obvious contrast

nodes.label: Write the CTA microcopy, not the button color
nodes.norm_label: write the cta microcopy, not the button color
nodes.rationale: The CTA label moves conversion far more than button color or shape — it's the last thing the user reads before deciding, so it must reduce the mental effort of simulating what happens next.
nodes.source_location: section: Write the CTA microcopy, not the button color

nodes.label: Charge your first ten users from day one
nodes.norm_label: charge your first ten users from day one
nodes.rationale: The first ten users define the product's entire curve, and payment is the cheapest test of real pain — curiosity is free, an open wallet demands a concrete problem.
nodes.source_location: section: Charge your first ten users from day one

nodes.label: Concentrate channels with the Bullseye framework, not scattershot testing
nodes.norm_label: concentrate channels with the bullseye framework, not scattershot testing
nodes.rationale: Testing ten channels at once means you never know what drove results and you blame the channel when the business stalls. Distribution needs prioritized focus — and a perfect channel still fails if the receiving structure leaks.
nodes.source_location: section: Concentrate channels with the Bullseye framework, not scattershot testing

nodes.label: Diagnose the bottleneck: no entries is distribution, leaving without paying is design
nodes.norm_label: diagnose the bottleneck: no entries is distribution, leaving without paying is design
nodes.rationale: Design can't save a "ghost product." Design optimizes and raises the LTV of something that already has traffic; it can't manufacture demand.
nodes.source_location: section: Diagnose the bottleneck: no entries is distribution, leaving without paying is design

nodes.label: Don't claim PLG without the four structural conditions
nodes.norm_label: don't claim plg without the four structural conditions
nodes.rationale: Product-led growth (PLG) is a consequence of structural conditions, not a product decision you declare. Most B2B SaaS that pitches PLG is really sales-led wearing a PLG label.
nodes.source_location: section: Don't claim PLG without the four structural conditions

nodes.label: Frame the referral prize as a gift to the friend, not a commission to the referrer
nodes.norm_label: frame the referral prize as a gift to the friend, not a commission to the referrer
nodes.rationale: Member-get-member (MGM) referral programs win on framing and timing, not just on a two-sided reward. Money makes the exchange feel transactional; an in-product benefit feels like a genuine gift.
nodes.source_location: section: Frame the referral prize as a gift to the friend, not a commission to the referrer

nodes.label: Pick a deliberately under-served niche as your ICP
nodes.norm_label: pick a deliberately under-served niche as your icp
nodes.rationale: A clear ICP (ideal customer profile) is not "everyone who could use my product." It's a deliberately chosen, under-served niche — and a sharp niche beats no niche, because you can't out-fight the entrenched generalist giant.
nodes.source_location: section: Pick a deliberately under-served niche as your ICP

nodes.label: Reverse-engineer the funnel math before celebrating an MRR target
nodes.norm_label: reverse-engineer the funnel math before celebrating an mrr target
nodes.rationale: Building the product is the easy part; distribution is the game. A revenue target is really a traffic-and-retention problem, and churn quietly resets the whole funnel every month.
nodes.source_location: section: Reverse-engineer the funnel math before celebrating an MRR target

nodes.label: Size the market with TAM → SAM → SOM (and know which one matters)
nodes.norm_label: size the market with tam → sam → som (and know which one matters)
nodes.rationale: Your real market is far smaller than the population — TAM is a theoretical ceiling (Brazil's 213M becomes ~101M credit-card holders for a paid app). Investors often ignore a TAM under ~R$1B, but the number that matters is the **SOM** — what you can actually capture.
nodes.source_location: section: Size the market with TAM → SAM → SOM (and know which one matters)

nodes.label: Architect for what users fear losing, not just what they gain
nodes.norm_label: architect for what users fear losing, not just what they gain
nodes.rationale: Builders obsess over features (gains), but conversion and retention are cemented by what the user fears losing — the pain of abandoning a built-up ecosystem outweighs the pain of paying a subscription.
nodes.source_location: section: Architect for what users fear losing, not just what they gain

nodes.label: Cut cognitive load — every choice you remove can lift conversion
nodes.norm_label: cut cognitive load — every choice you remove can lift conversion
nodes.rationale: Each extra field, choice, or block of complex text spends the user's mental energy and triggers analysis paralysis. Your product can be complex; your interface doesn't have to be.
nodes.source_location: section: Cut cognitive load — every choice you remove can lift conversion

nodes.label: Guide the eye — don't give every option equal weight
nodes.norm_label: guide the eye — don't give every option equal weight
nodes.rationale: The brain uses contrast to make fast decisions (Von Restorff effect). When competing options carry identical visual weight, you create mental friction, decision time rises, and conversion falls. Guiding the user isn't manipulation — it's respect for their time.
nodes.source_location: section: Guide the eye — don't give every option equal weight

nodes.label: Reinforce the decision the user just made
nodes.norm_label: reinforce the decision the user just made
nodes.rationale: After committing to a choice, people actively seek information that supports it — choice-supportive bias. You can feed that need to make the decision feel right.
nodes.source_location: section: Reinforce the decision the user just made

nodes.label: Set the default — it's the most underrated lever in conversion
nodes.norm_label: set the default — it's the most underrated lever in conversion
nodes.rationale: The pre-selected option captures the overwhelming majority of choices, because deciding is expensive and the lazy brain takes the easiest path. Smart defaults beat copy persuasion.
nodes.source_location: section: Set the default — it's the most underrated lever in conversion

nodes.label: Use precise numbers, not round ones, to signal truth
nodes.norm_label: use precise numbers, not round ones, to signal truth
nodes.rationale: Exact figures read as more credible than rounded ones; round numbers signal marketing while specific numbers signal reality.
nodes.source_location: section: Use precise numbers, not round ones, to signal truth

nodes.label: You can't un-hear your own product
nodes.norm_label: you can't un-hear your own product
nodes.rationale: Once you know how your product works, that knowledge permanently rewrites your perception — what feels obvious to you is just "tap-tap-tap" to a first-time user. You'll mistake confused users for dumb users.
nodes.source_location: section: You can't un-hear your own product

nodes.label: A validated idea is a short-term game — plan the moat
nodes.norm_label: a validated idea is a short-term game — plan the moat
nodes.rationale: If your only advantage is the codebase, you've merely built a validated MVP for better-funded competitors to execute. Structural barriers to entry (the moat) are planned, never accidental.
nodes.source_location: section: A validated idea is a short-term game — plan the moat

nodes.label: Beat the four AI failure modes that make a vibe-coded SaaS feel like a fraud
nodes.norm_label: beat the four ai failure modes that make a vibe-coded saas feel like a fraud
nodes.rationale: When the barrier to entry tends to zero, competition tends to infinity. AI lowered that barrier and amplified Dunning-Kruger — you feel omniscient but lack the base to judge if its output is a solution or wasted time. You shipped code, not a seductive product, and you're diving into a red ocean. Code is no longer the asset — just one ingredient.
nodes.source_location: section: Beat the four AI failure modes that make a vibe-coded SaaS feel like a fraud

nodes.label: Design for shrinking attention spans
nodes.rationale: Short-form video acts on the brain like a variable-reward slot machine, switching off the attention filter and eroding self-control — leaving users with high anxiety and low focus. If your user's attention keeps shrinking, design must be militarily focused.
nodes.source_location: section: Design for shrinking attention spans

nodes.label: Don't let AI-to-Figma-to-code factory technical debt
nodes.norm_label: don't let ai-to-figma-to-code factory technical debt
nodes.rationale: A Claude → Figma → Code flow looks like speed but creates two documents that drift out of sync, plus inconsistent components — a maintenance Frankenstein, not velocity.
nodes.source_location: section: Don't let AI-to-Figma-to-code factory technical debt

nodes.label: Faster building doesn't fix churn — activation does
nodes.norm_label: faster building doesn't fix churn — activation does
nodes.rationale: Build speed was never the bottleneck. Shipping the same confusing interface faster is just a more efficient route to churn. The real gap is the space between a user entering the product and understanding what to do.
nodes.source_location: section: Faster building doesn't fix churn — activation does

nodes.label: Same engine, different UX: don't compete on the commodity
nodes.norm_label: same engine, different ux: don't compete on the commodity
nodes.rationale: AI turned your codebase into a near-commodity — under the hood ~90% of new tools call the same APIs. Engineering solves the base function; design and packaging are what differentiate and resist copying.
nodes.source_location: section: Same engine, different UX: don't compete on the commodity

nodes.label: Sell the value, not the feature list — and show the product
nodes.norm_label: sell the value, not the feature list — and show the product
nodes.rationale: AI auto-generates landing pages, but ~90% share the same defects. A generic, inconsistent hero is what loses visitors, not the absence of fancy design.
nodes.source_location: section: Sell the value, not the feature list — and show the product

nodes.label: Celebrate signal quality, not list size
nodes.norm_label: celebrate signal quality, not list size
nodes.rationale: A waitlist exists to validate that a pain is one people pay to solve — not to sell. Absolute size is a vanity metric; conversion-weighted quality is the real signal.
nodes.source_location: section: Celebrate signal quality, not list size

nodes.label: Don't bet your product on an underpowered A/B test
nodes.norm_label: don't bet your product on an underpowered a/b test
nodes.rationale: Most A/B tests in small SaaS lack the volume to prove anything, yet founders swap the whole product on the result. Testing without enough sample to conclude is the trap.
nodes.source_location: section: Don't bet your product on an underpowered A/B test

nodes.label: Don't mistake signups for traction
nodes.rationale: Signups are the cheapest action a user takes, so they measure curiosity, not value — especially in freemium. Real growth is whether people come back and do the action that delivers value.
nodes.source_location: section: Don't mistake signups for traction

nodes.label: Duolingo's lesson: optimize the metric that moves DAU, not the borrowed mechanic
nodes.norm_label: duolingo's lesson: optimize the metric that moves dau, not the borrowed mechanic
nodes.rationale: Duolingo copied game mechanics twice and failed both (a Gardenscapes moves-counter: neutral; a referral program copied from Uber: +3% because the reward excluded the best users). They stopped picking mechanics and modeled which number to move: bucketing users by engagement and simulating +2%/quarter for 3 years, CURR (current-user retention rate) had ~5x the impact of the next-best metric. Then gamification worked: CURR +21% over 4 years, daily churn of best users −40%+, DAU ×4.5. Leaderboards alone +17% total learning time and tripled highly-engaged learners — because they switched to competing with users of *similar prior-week engagement* (auto opt-in = default effect, no extra tasks).
nodes.source_location: section: Duolingo's lesson: optimize the metric that moves DAU, not the borrowed mechanic

nodes.label: Nine product metrics, each telling one thing
nodes.norm_label: nine product metrics, each telling one thing
nodes.rationale: ARR = size (not necessarily health). Burn rate = risk (time until death). CAC = efficiency (but obsessing over lowering it can worsen conversion with a less-qualified cohort). DAU/MAU = engagement (<20% = bad sign). LTV = product (does the customer see value?). Churn = fit (user doesn't understand or see value → cancels). NRR = real growth (>100% = good). Gross margin = model (<70% in SaaS = problem, except AI wrappers). Runway = survival (<12 months = danger). Metrics are like a blood panel — one bad reading is critical, but all-good is real health.
nodes.source_location: section: Nine product metrics, each telling one thing

nodes.label: Translate churn points into LTV, not percentages
nodes.norm_label: translate churn points into ltv, not percentages
nodes.rationale: Most people watch churn %, but few compute what each point costs in accumulated LTV over 12 months. Cutting churn is a cash lever that needs no price hike or new acquisition.
nodes.source_location: section: Translate churn points into LTV, not percentages

nodes.label: 97% of visitors buy nothing — the leaks are known and fixable
nodes.norm_label: 97% of visitors buy nothing — the leaks are known and fixable
nodes.rationale: Cart abandonment reasons are mapped and mostly design-fixable: late extra costs (49%), forced account creation (24%), slow delivery (19%), complicated checkout (18%), distrust of the site (17%), unclear price (17%), site errors (12%), bad return policy (11%).
nodes.source_location: section: 97% of visitors buy nothing — the leaks are known and fixable

nodes.label: Checkout is where ~70% of drops happen — every extra input is less conversion
nodes.norm_label: checkout is where ~70% of drops happen — every extra input is less conversion
nodes.rationale: At checkout, less is more. Each extra input is less conversion; ask for the minimum possible. Any new negative surprise is a reason to cancel — expensive shipping, paid shipping at all, service fee, packaging fee — embed every extra charge into the product price, never as a hidden extra.
nodes.source_location: section: Checkout is where ~70% of drops happen — every extra input is less conversion

nodes.label: Friction kills conversion — field count, input type, and perceived risk all compound
nodes.norm_label: friction kills conversion — field count, input type, and perceived risk all compound
nodes.rationale: More fields = lower conversion, but the *type* of input matters too: text fields usually generate less impact, while dropdowns and textareas hurt more. Phone number drops conversion; any data that raises perceived risk or invasiveness does the same. And perceived effort ≠ real effort — 5 steps with 2 fields per screen can beat 2 screens with 7 fields each.
nodes.source_location: section: Friction kills conversion — field count, input type, and perceived risk all compound

nodes.label: Microcopy at the point of fraud risk beats friction everywhere else
nodes.norm_label: microcopy at the point of fraud risk beats friction everywhere else
nodes.rationale: Design must protect the user from the real environment the product lives in — especially in low-trust economies. One line of microcopy in the right place prevents scams that cost more than the friction of adding it.
nodes.source_location: section: Microcopy at the point of fraud risk beats friction everywhere else

nodes.label: You lose money on the boring screens
nodes.norm_label: you lose money on the boring screens
nodes.rationale: Registration forms are where you lose users one input at a time, creating holes in your bucket and wasting CAC — while founders polish the hero. The idea is to remove cognitive load until the flow is so smooth the user doesn't notice it.
nodes.source_location: section: You lose money on the boring screens

nodes.label: A good dashboard informs at a glance — like a car dashboard, the user must focus on where they're going
nodes.norm_label: a good dashboard informs at a glance — like a car dashboard, the user must focus on where they're going
nodes.rationale: A good dashboard is informative and effortless to read — the main KPI sits top-left (F-pattern), every element either earns its place or is noise. The goal isn't informing: it's eliminating churn and maximizing LTV through value so large the user feels the need to return.
nodes.source_location: section: A good dashboard informs at a glance — like a car dashboard, the user must focus on where they're going

nodes.label: Dashboards: not a pile of gauges — every extra indicator slows the scan for what's actionable
nodes.norm_label: dashboards: not a pile of gauges — every extra indicator slows the scan for what's actionable
nodes.rationale: The original "dashboard" was a board on carriages that kept horse mud off the passengers; the first Ford T kept the design with just an ignition key and an ammeter, and gauges accumulated from there. That industrial-era aesthetic survives in luxury cars and watches — the "complications" on a Patek Philippe or a Pagani — where it's interesting; in a software dashboard it isn't. The more information on screen, the higher the cognitive load and the longer it takes to scan for what is important and actionable. A good dashboard is built around the business's main indicators.

nodes.norm_label: removing information creates room for direction — the dashboard should say what to do with the data
nodes.rationale: Good product design work is mostly *removing*: showing less and giving clarity to what remains, based on what the user needs on that screen. Removing information opens space for direction — the app stops just showing data and starts saying what to do with it. That's the actionable layer.

nodes.label: Add declarative friction, cut administrative friction
nodes.norm_label: add declarative friction, cut administrative friction
nodes.rationale: "Good onboarding is short onboarding" is incomplete. There are two frictions: administrative (collects data the system uses later, buys the user nothing) and declarative (forces the user to state what they came to do — costs a beat, buys commitment, customization, and journey direction).
nodes.source_location: section: Add declarative friction, cut administrative friction

nodes.label: An onboarding video welcomes — it doesn't teach
nodes.norm_label: an onboarding video welcomes — it doesn't teach
nodes.rationale: A good onboarding video isn't a manual (nobody reads their car's or iPhone's). It welcomes, builds connection, shows the product at a glance, and points to where value comes fastest.
nodes.source_location: section: An onboarding video welcomes — it doesn't teach

nodes.label: Calibrate the first step to the user's real willingness
nodes.norm_label: calibrate the first step to the user's real willingness
nodes.rationale: Users don't rationally evaluate the first task — they evaluate perceived effort. Ask too much up front and the cognitive cost of even imagining the task is paralyzing, and they quit before starting. This is the activation-barrier effect.
nodes.source_location: section: Calibrate the first step to the user's real willingness

nodes.label: Celebrate the activation moment, don't just confirm it
nodes.norm_label: celebrate the activation moment, don't just confirm it
nodes.rationale: At the emotional peak of activation, a number is data but a rising graph is progress — and progress triggers dopamine and an emotional memory tied to the product. Most SaaS confirms where it should celebrate.
nodes.source_location: section: Celebrate the activation moment, don't just confirm it

nodes.label: Cut time-to-value by reorder and removal, not feature changes
nodes.norm_label: cut time-to-value by reorder and removal, not feature changes
nodes.rationale: High TTV is almost never product complexity — it's the form and order in which things happen. Each day between signup and first result is another day of abandonment risk; abandonment = churn.
nodes.source_location: section: Cut time-to-value by reorder and removal, not feature changes

nodes.label: Deliver the promised result before teaching mechanics
nodes.norm_label: deliver the promised result before teaching mechanics
nodes.rationale: Nobody wants to learn to use your product; they want the result you promised in the landing-page hero. Teaching mechanics first ("create a project → add a member → configure integrations") is boring; delivering value first converts.
nodes.source_location: section: Deliver the promised result before teaching mechanics

nodes.label: Design onboarding as a behavioral trigger, not a feature tour
nodes.norm_label: design onboarding as a behavioral trigger, not a feature tour
nodes.rationale: Silent non-activation — users who sign up, vanish in five minutes, and never formally churn — is an activation problem, not a product one. Onboarding should fire a behavior, not narrate features.
nodes.source_location: section: Design onboarding as a behavioral trigger, not a feature tour

nodes.label: Give the trial an active goal, not passive access
nodes.norm_label: give the trial an active goal, not passive access
nodes.rationale: A passive trial ("use it if you want, cancel guilt-free") builds no commitment; a trial with an active goal builds commitment before billing. Each completed day raises the psychological cost of canceling — the user starts defending a decision they already made, before paying.
nodes.source_location: section: Give the trial an active goal, not passive access

nodes.label: Make onboarding active, not passive
nodes.rationale: Passive onboarding (tooltips, guided tour, docs — learn if you want) assumes the user will explore. They won't: they have 47 tabs open, WhatsApp pinging, and will do the bare minimum before deciding whether to return. Active onboarding designs a sequence where each action delivers value and that value triggers the next.
nodes.source_location: section: Make onboarding active, not passive

nodes.label: Map the journey from session replays, not from your diagram
nodes.norm_label: map the journey from session replays, not from your diagram
nodes.rationale: The founder's 12-step journey is built top-down (what the product wants); the user runs 4 steps bottom-up (the specific problem they opened the tab to solve). The gap between them is where avoidable early-stage churn lives — and it's invisible because the founder only ever lived the creator's journey.
nodes.source_location: section: Map the journey from session replays, not from your diagram

nodes.label: Map the whole journey to value — then fix the biggest drop, not the first step
nodes.norm_label: map the whole journey to value — then fix the biggest drop, not the first step
nodes.rationale: Founders rush to the top of the funnel when activation falls, but the leak is usually in the middle — the step where effort is already high and the user hasn't seen proof it's worth it. Method: (1) Define what "value" is (the first moment the user gets the promised result — measurable, visible in data). (2) List every step between signup and that value (every screen, click, wait, field — always more than you remember). (3) Measure drop per step; find the steepest fall. (4) Fix the biggest drop first — that's where the money is. (5) Diagnose why: friction (cut), confusion (direct attention), ordering (deliver value before asking effort).
nodes.source_location: section: Map the whole journey to value — then fix the biggest drop, not the first step

nodes.label: Measure activation, not signups
nodes.rationale: Technical founders track the wrong onboarding metrics; signups, session time, and tour completion all flatter you without proving the user reached value.

nodes.label: Never ship a blank dashboard
nodes.rationale: The empty dashboard arrives at the user's peak of curiosity and answers it with a void — this is where most SaaS loses the trial. Every second spent deciding what to do is a second closer to quitting.
nodes.source_location: section: Never ship a blank dashboard

nodes.label: Pick onboarding patterns by awareness × flow complexity
nodes.norm_label: pick onboarding patterns by awareness × flow complexity
nodes.rationale: There's no best onboarding in the abstract — only the one that removes friction and delivers value early for your users. Treat the nine patterns as behavior-shaping mechanisms, not UI components, and select by two axes.
nodes.source_location: section: Pick onboarding patterns by awareness × flow complexity

nodes.label: Put friction in the right place, not zero friction everywhere
nodes.norm_label: put friction in the right place, not zero friction everywhere
nodes.rationale: Friction in the wrong place kills the product; friction in the right place qualifies and retains. "Less friction" is not a universal law.
nodes.source_location: section: Put friction in the right place, not zero friction everywhere

nodes.label: Qualify by behavior, not by a long signup form
nodes.norm_label: qualify by behavior, not by a long signup form
nodes.rationale: Friction at the wrong moment kills conversion, and qualification by behavior is more precise than qualification by form. The "more qualified leads" argument for long forms usually loses.
nodes.source_location: section: Qualify by behavior, not by a long signup form

nodes.label: Rising MRR with rising churn means you lost them on day one
nodes.norm_label: rising mrr with rising churn means you lost them on day one
nodes.rationale: When MRR and churn climb together, the user didn't leave in month 2 — they were lost the first day, dropped into a dead empty-state dashboard with nothing guiding them to value.
nodes.source_location: section: Rising MRR with rising churn means you lost them on day one

nodes.label: Treat onboarding as the bridge between CAC and LTV
nodes.norm_label: treat onboarding as the bridge between cac and ltv
nodes.rationale: Founders obsess over CAC and landing-page conversion but are blind to activation cost. Onboarding isn't an interface tutorial — it's the bridge from CAC to LTV and the point of maximum leverage to expand revenue. Cancellation happens on day one; it's merely formalized when Stripe's billing reminder lands.
nodes.source_location: section: Treat onboarding as the bridge between CAC and LTV

nodes.label: Treat sub-30-day churn as an onboarding fix, not a feature gap
nodes.norm_label: treat sub-30-day churn as an onboarding fix, not a feature gap
nodes.rationale: Most early-stage SaaS churn happens in the first 30 days — which means it's onboarding, not product. Adding features only makes it worse by adding complexity.
nodes.source_location: section: Treat sub-30-day churn as an onboarding fix, not a feature gap

nodes.label: Trial conversion is a journey problem, not a pricing problem
nodes.norm_label: trial conversion is a journey problem, not a pricing problem
nodes.rationale: A trial is a test of value; if the user never proves value to themselves, no price or trial length saves it. Conversion fails for three diagnosable reasons.
nodes.source_location: section: Trial conversion is a journey problem, not a pricing problem
